ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: This study conformed to the principles outlined by the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by University of Tasmania Human Research Ethics Committee (Approval Number 27255).

Stroop tasks present stimuli composed of at least two distinct features: the response stimulus (S r ), which is the task-relevant feature participants are instructed to respond to, and the task-irrelevant stimulus (S i ), which must be ignored (see MacLeod, 1991 MacLeod,, 2005 for review) for review).
table.formatted: Stroop tasks present stimuli composed of at least two distinct features: the response stimulus (S r ), which is the task-relevant feature participants are instructed to respond to, and the task-irrelevant stimulus (S i ), which must be ignored (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">MacLeod, 1991</ref> <ref type="bibr">MacLeod, , 2005 for review) for review)</ref>.

table.text: Indeed, in the classic colour-word Stroop task participants are faster at reading printed words than they are at naming colours.
Participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, were free from known neurological conditions and could read and write fluently in English.
Participants were either a convenience sample recruited via word of mouth, or recruited through the University of Tasmania's Research Participation system for students.
All participants provided written consent prior to participation.
Participants were seated approximately 60cm from a 25" computer monitor (1920 x 1080, 60Hz) with their forearms resting on a desk.

Prior to each condition, participants were informed via an instruction screen whether their upcoming goal was to respond to either the word ("LEFT" or "RIGHT") or the arrow direction (ß or à) -the S r, and they were reminded what their response would be (button press for the manual conditions, or spoken response in the vocal conditions).

In Mixed conditions, to minimise anticipation, participants were not informed of the proportion of congruent to incongruent trials, only to "respond to the direction of the Stimulus and Response Conditions Note.

Given that participants were slower and made more errors on incongruent trials when responding manually to the word in Mixed conditions compared to Pure blocks, our findings support this view that inhibition reflects two concurrent mechanisms: resolving interference at the trial level and maintaining task goals across trials.

Given that our participants were an educated, English-speaking, convenience sample, the impact of reading fluency was likely reflected in our relatively small proportion of errors and corrections observed in the vocal task.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 4 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  2 files skipped as byte-identical duplicates of another file already in the run (the paper links more than one repository/component).
-  1 of 2 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  9 installable dependencies detected.
- 1216 statistics stored from the extracted output; 8 of 24 reported tests matched (33.3%).

live_data_statements: Stroop tasks present stimuli composed of at least two distinct features: the response stimulus (S r ), which is the task-relevant feature participants are instructed to respond to, and the task-irrelevant stimulus (S i ), which must be ignored (see MacLeod, 1991 MacLeod,, 2005 for review) for review).
Indeed, in the classic colour-word Stroop task participants are faster at reading printed words than they are at naming colours.
Participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, were free from known neurological conditions and could read and write fluently in English.
Participants were either a convenience sample recruited via word of mouth, or recruited through the University of Tasmania's Research Participation system for students.
All participants provided written consent prior to participation.
Participants were seated approximately 60cm from a 25" computer monitor (1920 x 1080, 60Hz) with their forearms resting on a desk.

Prior to each condition, participants were informed via an instruction screen whether their upcoming goal was to respond to either the word ("LEFT" or "RIGHT") or the arrow direction (ß or à) -the S r, and they were reminded what their response would be (button press for the manual conditions, or spoken response in the vocal conditions).

In Mixed conditions, to minimise anticipation, participants were not informed of the proportion of congruent to incongruent trials, only to "respond to the direction of the Stimulus and Response Conditions Note.

Given that participants were slower and made more errors on incongruent trials when responding manually to the word in Mixed conditions compared to Pure blocks, our findings support this view that inhibition reflects two concurrent mechanisms: resolving interference at the trial level and maintaining task goals across trials.

Given that our participants were an educated, English-speaking, convenience sample, the impact of reading fluency was likely reflected in our relatively small proportion of errors and corrections observed in the vocal task.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order

No ordering signal (no data dependency, `source()` call, or numeric filename prefix) distinguishes the run order of these files. They may need to run in a specific order that could not be determined automatically — check this before running.

```{r}

"Vocal_Task_AnalysisCode.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—"), 
    Basis = c("none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `C:/OSF/Data/Task_B_data.csv` to `../Data/Task_B_data.csv` (in Vocal_Task_AnalysisCode.R); `C:/OSF/Data/Task_A_data.csv` to `../Data/Task_A_data.csv` (in Manual_Task_AnalysisCode.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 1 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

text.text: The arrow-word Stroop task measures inhibitory control by assessing the slowing of vocal responses to arrow direction when paired with an incongruent word (e.g., 'LEFT' printed on a right-pointing arrow).
This interference is commonly attributed to the automaticity of word reading.
However, the same pattern is not observed with manual responses, suggesting modality influences interference.
We investigated competing theoretical accounts by systematically manipulating the task-relevant stimulus and response modality.
Thirty-two participants (18-52 years) completed two Stroop variants using either manual left/right button presses, or vocal "left"/"right" responses.

In each condition the task-relevant stimulus was either the arrow or word, and performance in Pure (100% congruent or incongruent trials) and Mixed (66% congruent, 33% incongruent) blocks were compared with Baseline blocks.
Vocal responses were faster to words than arrows, and incongruent words slowed responses to arrows, but arrow direction did not affect word responses.
This pattern reversed for manual responses: button presses were faster to arrows than words, with incongruent arrows slowing word responses.

These findings challenge accounts attributing Stroop interference to automatic word processing, instead suggesting interference arises when the task-relevant stimulus requires translation into the response modality while the irrelevant dimension is more directly compatible with that response.

Suppressing the urge to check a phone notification while studying, or refraining from swearing at work, are everyday examples of inhibitory control: a key executive function that suppresses impulsive or prepotent responses in favour of more appropriate or goal-directed behaviours (Diamond, 2013).
text.formatted: Suppressing the urge to check a phone notification while studying, or refraining from swearing at work, are everyday examples of inhibitory control: a key executive function that suppresses impulsive or prepotent responses in favour of more appropriate or goal-directed behaviours <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Diamond, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Cognitive inhibition, which involves suppressing interference from over-learned responses, is commonly assessed with the Stroop task (Stroop, 1935).
text.formatted: Cognitive inhibition, which involves suppressing interference from over-learned responses, is commonly assessed with the Stroop task <ref type="bibr">(Stroop, 1935)</ref>.

text.text: Stroop interference refers to the decrement in performance (i.e. slower responses or increased errors) that occurs when an irrelevant stimulus (typically the presence of a word) interferes with the response required by the task (typically naming the colour the word is printed in).
Despite being studied for almost a century, the mechanisms responsible for the interference remains debated (Macleod, 1991).
text.formatted: Despite being studied for almost a century, the mechanisms responsible for the interference remains debated <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Macleod, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Traditional accounts emphasise the automaticity of word reading, whereas alternative accounts suggest that interference is determined by how readily competing stimulus dimensions map onto the required response.

The arrow-word Stroop task provides a means of investigating these accounts because both the task-relevant stimulus dimension (respond to the word meaning versus arrow direction) and response modality (vocal versus manual button pressing) can be independently manipulated, yet few studies have systematically examined these factors within the same experiment.
Beyond its theoretical importance, Stroop paradigms also have clinical relevance, with subtle impairments in performance observed in preclinical Alzheimer's Disease (AD) (Wells et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Beyond its theoretical importance, Stroop paradigms also have clinical relevance, with subtle impairments in performance observed in preclinical Alzheimer's Disease (AD) <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Wells et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, common Stroop paradigms require participants to produce spoken responses, making it difficult to distinguish impaired cognitive inhibition from impairments in speech production (Ivanova et al., 2024).
text.formatted: However, common Stroop paradigms require participants to produce spoken responses, making it difficult to distinguish impaired cognitive inhibition from impairments in speech production <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ivanova et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Speech becomes slower and more error-prone with ageing (Gollan & Goldrick, 2019), and is further impaired in neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's Disease (PD) (Mu et al., 2024) and AD (Gerstner et al., 2007; Martínez-Nicolás et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Speech becomes slower and more error-prone with ageing <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Gollan & Goldrick, 2019)</ref>, and is further impaired in neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's Disease (PD) <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Mu et al., 2024)</ref> and AD <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gerstner et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Martínez-Nicolás et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A manual Stroop paradigm could therefore reduce the influence of speech-related impairments, provide more precise measurement of response times than voice-based response detection, and facilitate remote or online assessment.

Although other inhibitory paradigms such as the Simon (Simon & Rudell, 1967) , and Flanker tasks (Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974) use manual button presses, they assess different forms of conflict and so cannot directly substitute for Stroop interference (Egner et al., 2007; Scerrati et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Although other inhibitory paradigms such as the Simon <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Simon & Rudell, 1967)</ref> , and Flanker tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974)</ref> use manual button presses, they assess different forms of conflict and so cannot directly substitute for Stroop interference <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Egner et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Scerrati et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, establishing how Stroop interference operates with manual responses has both theoretical and potential clinical value.

Stroop tasks present stimuli composed of at least two distinct features: the response stimulus (S r ), which is the task-relevant feature participants are instructed to respond to, and the task-irrelevant stimulus (S i ), which must be ignored (see MacLeod, 1991 MacLeod, , 2005 for review) for review).
text.formatted: Stroop tasks present stimuli composed of at least two distinct features: the response stimulus (S r ), which is the task-relevant feature participants are instructed to respond to, and the task-irrelevant stimulus (S i ), which must be ignored (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">MacLeod, 1991</ref> <ref type="bibr">MacLeod, , 2005 for review) for review)</ref>.

text.text: In the classic colour-word Stroop Task (Stroop, 1935), participants name aloud the ink colour of a written word (S r ) and attempt to suppress the tendency to say the written word (S i ); for example, responding "blue" to the word 'RED' printed in blue ink.
text.formatted: In the classic colour-word Stroop Task <ref type="bibr">(Stroop, 1935)</ref>, participants name aloud the ink colour of a written word (S r ) and attempt to suppress the tendency to say the written word (S i ); for example, responding "blue" to the word 'RED' printed in blue ink.

text.text: Stroop interference refers to slower or less accurate responses on incongruent trials, in which S i and S r conflict, relative to a neutral baseline condition (e.g., naming the colour of 'XXXX').

Conversely, Stroop facilitation refers to faster or more accurate responses on congruent trials, in which S i and S r correspond (e.g., saying "red" when presented with the word 'RED' in red ink) compared to baseline (Macleod, 1991).
text.formatted: Conversely, Stroop facilitation refers to faster or more accurate responses on congruent trials, in which S i and S r correspond (e.g., saying "red" when presented with the word 'RED' in red ink) compared to baseline <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Macleod, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Although the classic colour-word Stroop task typically requires verbal responses, manual versions that require arbitrary stimulus-response mappings (e.g., press the 'F' key for blue), are also used.
These tasks introduce additional response-rule learning demands and produce diminished interference effects.

The arrow-word Stroop task (Baldo et al., 1998; Besner et al., 2026; Luo & Proctor, 2013), is an alternative that overcomes this limitation, whereby words with a directional meaning (e.g., 'LEFT' or 'RIGHT') are presented within arrow symbols pointing left or right, thus stimulus features may be congruent (e.g.
text.formatted: The arrow-word Stroop task <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baldo et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Besner et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Luo & Proctor, 2013)</ref>, is an alternative that overcomes this limitation, whereby words with a directional meaning (e.g., 'LEFT' or 'RIGHT') are presented within arrow symbols pointing left or right, thus stimulus features may be congruent (e.g.

text.text: 'LEFT' presented within a left arrow) or incongruent (e.g.
'LEFT' presented within a right arrow).

Previous manual arrow-word Stroop studies suggest that interference patterns do not align with traditional vocal task, as the arrows disrupt responses to words more than words disrupt responses to arrows (Baldo et al., 1998; Besner et al., 2025; Luo & Proctor, 2013).
text.formatted: Previous manual arrow-word Stroop studies suggest that interference patterns do not align with traditional vocal task, as the arrows disrupt responses to words more than words disrupt responses to arrows <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baldo et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Besner et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Luo & Proctor, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that Stroop interference does not strictly depend on the automaticity of word reading.

As either dimension can serve as the task-relevant stimulus, the Stroop arrow-word paradigm provides a useful framework for systematically manipulating stimulus-response compatibility to evaluate competing theoretical models.
A simple, response speed account (Figure 1A) suggests that the cognitive process that yields faster responses should be considered as more automatic.
text.formatted: A simple, response speed account (Figure <ref type="figure">1A</ref>) suggests that the cognitive process that yields faster responses should be considered as more automatic.

text.text: On the basis of this view, interference in incongruent scenarios is maximal when the stimulus associated with the slower (less automatic) process is nominated as the responding stimulus (S r ), such that the capacity to override the faster, more automatic process (S i ) can be measured in terms of changes to response speed and accuracy (Morton & Chambers, 1973).
text.formatted: On the basis of this view, interference in incongruent scenarios is maximal when the stimulus associated with the slower (less automatic) process is nominated as the responding stimulus (S r ), such that the capacity to override the faster, more automatic process (S i ) can be measured in terms of changes to response speed and accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Morton & Chambers, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, in the classic colour-word Stroop task participants are faster at reading printed words than they are at naming colours.

Thus, when responding to the stimulus feature that relies on the less automatic process (i.e., colour naming) and ignoring the stimulus that engages the more automatic process (i.e., word reading) responses are slowed and less accurate on incongruent trials (interference) or hastened and more accurate on congruent trials (facilitation).

In contrast, for the reverse configuration -when the response is to the more automatic process (word reading) -the less automatic stimulus feature (ink colour) produces no interference (or facilitation).
This unidirectional pattern is referred to as the asymmetry of the Stroop effect.

Word-reading may be a special case of stimulus processing as, in skilled adult readers, it is thought to operate automatically as an overlearned skill that is difficult to voluntarily suppress (see Besner et al., 1997 for review; Samuels & Flor, 1997).
text.formatted: Word-reading may be a special case of stimulus processing as, in skilled adult readers, it is thought to operate automatically as an overlearned skill that is difficult to voluntarily suppress (see <ref type="bibr">Besner et al., 1997 for review;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Samuels & Flor, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: According to the reading automaticity model (Figure 1B), the meaning of a written word is activated involuntarily upon presentation, regardless of whether it is relevant to the task.
text.formatted: According to the reading automaticity model (Figure <ref type="figure">1B</ref>), the meaning of a written word is activated involuntarily upon presentation, regardless of whether it is relevant to the task.

text.text: This prediction is supported by findings of the verbal colour-word Stroop paradigm (see Macleod, 1991 for review), and studies of priming that show that word reading is relatively unaffected by other top-down cognitive processes (Tse & Neely, 2007).
text.formatted: This prediction is supported by findings of the verbal colour-word Stroop paradigm (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Macleod, 1991</ref> for review), and studies of priming that show that word reading is relatively unaffected by other top-down cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Tse & Neely, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: According to the reading automaticity model, Stroop effect asymmetry should be observed regardless of response modality (i.e., whether responses are vocal or manual) since word reading dominates other stimulus dimensions.
However, evidence from both the colour-word and arrow-word Stroop tasks challenge this view.

When responses are manual, interference is markedly reduced in the colour-word Stroop task and the direction of interference is reversed entirely in the arrow-word Stroop task -with arrows interfering more with responses to words (Baldo et al., 1998; Besner et al., 2026).
text.formatted: When responses are manual, interference is markedly reduced in the colour-word Stroop task and the direction of interference is reversed entirely in the arrow-word Stroop task -with arrows interfering more with responses to words <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baldo et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Besner et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These findings are at odds with the idea that word reading is always the more automatic process, challenging strictly stimulus-driven accounts of interference and instead pointing to an interaction between stimulus processing and response selection mechanisms.

The Translation Model (Virzi & Egeth, 1985), proposes that interference between the S i and S r depends on the extent to which the task-relevant stimulus must be translated into the required response format.
text.formatted: The Translation Model <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Virzi & Egeth, 1985)</ref>, proposes that interference between the S i and S r depends on the extent to which the task-relevant stimulus must be translated into the required response format.

text.text: By this model, interference is predicted to be greatest when the task-relevant stimulus dimension requires translation into the response modality and reduced when stimulus and response formats correspond directly (Virzi & Egeth, 1985).
text.formatted: By this model, interference is predicted to be greatest when the task-relevant stimulus dimension requires translation into the response modality and reduced when stimulus and response formats correspond directly <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Virzi & Egeth, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: The Translation Model therefore makes similar predictions to the Response Speed account for the arrow-word Stroop task (Figure 1A) with manual responses to words slowed by the presence of incongruent arrows (Baldo et al., 1998; Besner et al., 2026; Luo & Proctor, 2013) consistent with the arrows interfering with the translation of word meaning into spatial coordinates needed to respond.
text.formatted: The Translation Model therefore makes similar predictions to the Response Speed account for the arrow-word Stroop task (Figure <ref type="figure">1A</ref>) with manual responses to words slowed by the presence of incongruent arrows <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baldo et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Besner et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Luo & Proctor, 2013)</ref> consistent with the arrows interfering with the translation of word meaning into spatial coordinates needed to respond.

text.text: Likewise, saying aloud the direction that an arrow is pointing is predicted to be slowed by the presence of incongruent words (Baldo et al., 1998; Besner et al., 2026; Shor, 1970; Shor et al., 1972) -consistent with interference in the language centres needed for the translation of spatial arrow cues into spoken responses.
text.formatted: Likewise, saying aloud the direction that an arrow is pointing is predicted to be slowed by the presence of incongruent words <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baldo et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Besner et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Shor, 1970;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Shor et al., 1972)</ref> -consistent with interference in the language centres needed for the translation of spatial arrow cues into spoken responses.

text.text: However, evidence from the less-studied stimulus-response compatible conditions (where translation is minimised) casts some doubt on the Translation model, as incongruent words have been shown to slightly slow manual responses to arrows relative to congruent words (Aarts et al., 2009; Baldo et al., 1998; Roelofs et al., 2006), while incongruent (relative to congruent) arrows have slowed verbal responses to words in one study (Baldo et al. 1998).
text.formatted: However, evidence from the less-studied stimulus-response compatible conditions (where translation is minimised) casts some doubt on the Translation model, as incongruent words have been shown to slightly slow manual responses to arrows relative to congruent words <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aarts et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Baldo et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Roelofs et al., 2006)</ref>, while incongruent (relative to congruent) arrows have slowed verbal responses to words in one study <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baldo et al. 1998)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that Stroop interference effects may not always be asymmetrical, as predicted by the Translation Model.
Symmetrical interference effects -where both stimulus features disrupt responding, are predicted by the Dimensional Overlap Model (DOM; Figure 1C; (Kornblum et al., 1990).
text.formatted: Symmetrical interference effects -where both stimulus features disrupt responding, are predicted by the Dimensional Overlap Model (DOM; Figure <ref type="figure">1C</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kornblum et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: The DOM proposes that interference occurs when an irrelevant stimulus dimension shares representational overlap with the relevant stimulus (stimulus-stimulus; S-S overlap), and/or activates a competing response (stimulus-response; S-R overlap).
In the arrow-word Stroop task, both arrow direction and word meaning convey spatial information, producing S-S overlap across both manual and verbal responding.
With manual responding, both dimensions also map onto spatial left/right actions, producing S-R overlap for both relevant and irrelevant stimuli.
Accordingly, the DOM predicts bidirectional and symmetrical interference: incongruent arrows should disrupt responses to words, and incongruent words should similarly disrupt responses to arrows.

Previous manual response arrow-word Stroop studies provide partial support for this prediction, with interference reported in both directions, but not necessarily to an equivalent magnitude; interference from arrows when responding to words is typically greater than interference from words when responding to arrows (Baldo et al., 1998; Roelofs et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Previous manual response arrow-word Stroop studies provide partial support for this prediction, with interference reported in both directions, but not necessarily to an equivalent magnitude; interference from arrows when responding to words is typically greater than interference from words when responding to arrows <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baldo et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Roelofs et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, for vocal responses, word stimuli map directly onto spoken responses ("left", "right"), whereas arrows do not.

This asymmetry in S-R overlap leads the DOM to predict the traditional asymmetrical interference for vocal responding, with incongruent words disrupting arrow naming, but incongruent arrows producing little interference during word reading (Shor, 1970).
text.formatted: This asymmetry in S-R overlap leads the DOM to predict the traditional asymmetrical interference for vocal responding, with incongruent words disrupting arrow naming, but incongruent arrows producing little interference during word reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Shor, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: Note.
Model predictions for interference across response mode and stimulus type.

When both response mode (vocal or manual) and response stimulus (word or arrow) are manipulated, different theoretical accounts predict distinct patterns of performance A. A simple model of response speed that assumes the faster the speed of the response to the baseline stimulus, the more automatic the process when both features are co-occurring, the Translation Model also has the same predictions; B. predictions from the theory that reading is the more automatic process regardless of response mode; and C. predictions of the Dimension Overlap Model.
Blue dots represent the baseline condition, green dots when the to-be-ignored stimulus is congruent with the target, and red dots when the to-be-ignored stimulus is incongruent with the target.
Higher dots indicate relatively faster response times, whereas lower dots indicate relatively slower response times.

Performance on Stroop tasks is thought to require two complementary processes: resolving interference on individual trials and maintaining task-goals across trials (goal maintenance) (Bélanger et al., 2010; Kane et al., 2007; Kane & Engle, 2003).
text.formatted: Performance on Stroop tasks is thought to require two complementary processes: resolving interference on individual trials and maintaining task-goals across trials (goal maintenance) <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bélanger et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kane et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kane & Engle, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Resolving triallevel interference involves suppressing the competing response activated by the irrelevant stimulus dimension.
Whereas, goal-maintenance keeps attention directed towards the taskrelevant dimension (Kane & Engle, 2003).
text.formatted: Whereas, goal-maintenance keeps attention directed towards the taskrelevant dimension <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Kane & Engle, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: These processes are considered distinct but complementary aspects of inhibitory control which may be differentially engaged depending on how different trial-types are structured within a block.
In Pure-block designs, a single trial type is presented (i.e. 100% congruent or 100% incongruent trials), allowing stable expectations and strategic responding.

For Pure incongruent blocks participants may exploit the S i as a reliable cue to predict the correct response, or use strategic responding (e.g., squint their eyes to minimise interference from the word in order to respond to stimulus features that are just as salient when acuity is diminished, such as arrow direction or font colour).
In this way, Pure blocks are thought to be less taxing on goal-maintenance demands.
In Mixed blocks, congruent and incongruent trials are randomly interleaved, reducing predictability and increasing goal-maintenance requirements.

A higher proportion of congruent trials has been found to reinforce the inappropriate response more often; thus, when an incongruent trial is presented, participants must use goal-maintenance to adhere to the correct task goal, limiting reliance on strategic responding (Logan & Zbrodoff, 1979).
text.formatted: A higher proportion of congruent trials has been found to reinforce the inappropriate response more often; thus, when an incongruent trial is presented, participants must use goal-maintenance to adhere to the correct task goal, limiting reliance on strategic responding <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Logan & Zbrodoff, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: Although the effect of different block structures has been studied and reviewed in the classic colour-word Stroop paradigms (Bélanger et al., 2010; Kane & Engle, 2003; Logan & Zbrodoff, 1979), it is unknown if a similar pattern of responses occurs in the arrow-word Stroop task.
text.formatted: Although the effect of different block structures has been studied and reviewed in the classic colour-word Stroop paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bélanger et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kane & Engle, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Logan & Zbrodoff, 1979)</ref>, it is unknown if a similar pattern of responses occurs in the arrow-word Stroop task.

text.text: Comparing performance on Pure and Mixed blocks in the arrow-word Stroop task allows the opportunity to assess whether interference patterns predicted by theoretical models remain consistent when goal-maintenance demands vary and determine how block structure modulates interference across response modalities during this task.

Thus, this study systematically examined the arrow-word Stroop task to investigate how the dynamics of stimulus-response mapping influences interference and facilitation processes separately for manual and vocal responses and compared the findings to theoretical model predictions (depicted in Figure 1) in both Pure-and Mixed-block designs.
text.formatted: Thus, this study systematically examined the arrow-word Stroop task to investigate how the dynamics of stimulus-response mapping influences interference and facilitation processes separately for manual and vocal responses and compared the findings to theoretical model predictions (depicted in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>) in both Pure-and Mixed-block designs.

text.text: Identifying these effects will determine which task configuration most strongly engage inhibitory processes.

The findings are relevant for future use of the manual arrow-word Stroop task to assess inhibitory ability in ageing and AD populations, where traditional vocal Stroop responses may be compromised or impractical, likely contributing to the tasks' limited application in these populations (Wells et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The findings are relevant for future use of the manual arrow-word Stroop task to assess inhibitory ability in ageing and AD populations, where traditional vocal Stroop responses may be compromised or impractical, likely contributing to the tasks' limited application in these populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Wells et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Healthy adults (N = 32, mean (SD) age, 32.5 (10.4) yrs, range, 18 -52; 22 female, 10 male), took part in two versions of the arrow-word Stroop task; a manual task involving leftright button press responses, and a vocal task involving spoken responses.
Participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, were free from known neurological conditions and could read and write fluently in English.
Participants were either a convenience sample recruited via word of mouth, or recruited through the University of Tasmania's Research Participation system for students.
All participants provided written consent prior to participation.
This study conformed to the principles outlined by the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by University of Tasmania Human Research Ethics Committee (Approval Number 27255).
Participants were seated approximately 60cm from a 25" computer monitor (1920 x 1080, 60Hz) with their forearms resting on a desk.
Custom-written software in MATLAB (2023a) running Psychtoolbox-3 (Version 3.0.19) presented visual stimuli on the screen.

As shown in Figure 2, the manual task required participants to respond by pressing keyboard buttons with either their left or right index fingers, whereas the vocal task required participants to respond by saying either "left" or "right".
text.formatted: As shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>, the manual task required participants to respond by pressing keyboard buttons with either their left or right index fingers, whereas the vocal task required participants to respond by saying either "left" or "right".

text.text: For both tasks, each of the eight conditions shown in Table 1 were randomly intermingled for each participant equating to 16 unique variations across both modalities.

text.text: The two response modalities were analysed separately due to differences in stimulus presentation and data collection variables.

Prior to each condition, participants were informed via an instruction screen whether their upcoming goal was to respond to either the word ("LEFT" or "RIGHT") or the arrow direction (ß or à) -the S r , and they were reminded what their response would be (button press for the manual conditions, or spoken response in the vocal conditions).
Participants undertook a series of practice trials at the beginning of each condition until they, and the experimenter, felt they understood and were comfortable with the task (between 4-6 trials).

Participants rested their left index finger on the "F" key and their right index finger on the "J" key of a standard QWERTY keyboard and were instructed to respond to stimuli presented on the screen with a left or right button press as 'quickly and as accurately possible'.
Across all trials in all conditions, a fixation cross (+) was presented in the centre of the screen before the imperative 'Go' stimulus.
The fixation cue was displayed for a time period randomly selected from a truncated exponential distribution between 0.5s to 1.0s to minimise proactive response anticipation.
Feedback was displayed for 1.0s duration after a 0.8sec response time window.
If the participant failed to respond within 0.8s, the feedback was 'Go faster'.

If they responded with the correct button press within the 0.8s window, the feedback was 'Correct, RT = [x]ms' (where x was the time from Go stimulus presentation to button press); if they responded with the incorrect button press, the feedback was a reminder of the instructed S r , either, "Respond to the Word", or "Respond to the Arrow".

For the manual button press conditions, there were 46 trials in each of the two baseline (Conditions 1, 2), Pure Congruent (Conditions 3, 4), and Pure Incongruent (Conditions 5, 6) conditions; there were 54 trials in each of the Mixed conditions (Conditions 7, 8), 36 of which were congruent and 18 incongruent (66.66% and 33.33% respectively).
This totalled 384 trials, excluding practice.
No other trials were excluded from analyses.
One participant did not complete Condition 5 (Incongruent S r Arrow) due to an equipment error.

The same eight Conditions in the manual response task were performed in the vocal response task; however, rather than pressing a button, participants vocalised the direction by saying "left", or "right" aloud (Figure 2B).
text.formatted: The same eight Conditions in the manual response task were performed in the vocal response task; however, rather than pressing a button, participants vocalised the direction by saying "left", or "right" aloud (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref>).

text.text: All 48 stimuli within a condition for the vocal task were presented in 6 rows of 8 stimuli on a single screen displayed on the 25" monitor.

The size of the stimuli was equivalent between manual and vocal responses, but the format for the vocal response task resembled the standard paper-based Stroop procedure commonly used in clinical and experimental contexts.
This format was chosen to allow comparability with the existing vocal Stroop literature.

Because the primary aim was to compare interference and facilitation effects within each response modality across stimulus and block conditions, rather than make absolute comparisons in response speed between manual and vocal tasks, differences in presentation format were not expected to influence the theoretical predictions under investigation.
Within each vocal Condition, participants spoke aloud their responses to each stimulus, moving from left-to-right through each row, and then onto subsequent rows until they completed all items.
As in the manual tasks, the vocal task also comprised a total of 384 trials excluding practice.
In the Mixed blocks, 32 trials were congruent and 16 incongruent (66.66% and 33.33% respectively).
Each participant saw the same sequence of cues for each of the eight conditions.

The sequence of trials was pseudorandomised so that 1) the correct response was not the same (left or right) for more than 4 trials in a row, and 2) the directions represented by the stimuli were equally presented (i.e., for 50% of the stimuli the correct response would be "left", and 50% "right").
Other than practice trials, no trials were excluded from analyses.

Data for both manual and vocal responses were analysed separately using R version 4.4.1 (R Core Team, 2024).
Random intercepts were always included in the statistical models, but random slopes were included only when the model still converged, and the AIC value was reduced (i.e. improved model-fit).
All models were fit using the bobyqa optimizer with increased optimisation iterations to aid convergence (Powell, 2009).

For interpretability, model estimates were back-transformed from the log scale.
Accuracy of responding was analysed using a GLMM with a binomial distribution and logit link function.
The dependent variable was the binary indicator (errors), coded 1 for incorrect (no response, or inaccurate response) and 0 for correct responses.
Participant ID was included as a random intercept (AIC = 2205.02); a random slope for Trial Type was also added (AIC = 2213.80) but did not significantly improve model-fit (χ²(5) = 1.21, p = .944).
Custom contrasts matched those used in the RT model, with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons.

The total time to complete the 48 trials of each block condition (ms) was measured from the onset of the vocal response to the first stimulus to the offset of the final vocal response (48 th stimulus).
Audio waveform and spectrograms in Audacity (Version 3.3.3) were used to identify the first detectable deviation from baseline (i.e., silence) corresponding to speech production.
The end of the block was marked by the return to baseline (silence) following the last response.

Corrected responses were also identified, where a participant began to make an error before correcting their vocal response (e.g., "Le-RIGHT" or "Ri -LEFT").

Total time for each condition was averaged between raters and divided by the total number of completed trials (i.e., excluding missed trials, while including correct, incorrect and corrected trials) to yield a mean RT per participant, per trial for each condition type.

To summarise the detailed comparisons below, manual button-press responses were faster to arrows than words, with an asymmetrical interference pattern: incongruent arrows interfered with responses to words, particularly in Mixed blocks, whereas incongruent words did not significantly interfere with responses to arrows.

Vocal responses showed the reverse pattern: responses were faster to words than arrows, with incongruent words interfering with responses to arrows, but incongruent arrows not interfering with responses to words.

This study provides a novel examination of how stimulus-response (S-R) compatibility influences interference and facilitation effects in the arrow-word Stroop task.

By systematically manipulating response modality (button press, vocal), response stimulus (arrow, word), and block structure (Pure, Mixed blocks), we tested competing theoretical accounts of Stroop interference and facilitation.

Importantly, these differing accounts make specific predictions about the pattern of interference within each response modality rather than absolute differences in response speed between manual and vocal responding.

A clear crossover pattern emerged: interference occurred in S-R incompatible conditions, when responding vocally to arrows or with button presses to words, but not in S-R compatible conditions, when responding vocally to words or with button presses to arrows.

Block structure further modulated these effects, with greater interference in Mixed than Pure blocks. predictions of the Response Speed, Translational Model, the automaticity of word reading account, and DOM.
Model Predictions of Stroop Effects compared to Results Note.
Model predictions (A,B,C from Figure 1) compared to the pattern of the observed results (D).
The baseline conditions provide clear evidence that S-R compatibility determines the relative speed of responding.

In baseline conditions participants responded fastest and more accurately when the stimulus dimension (S r ) matched the response modality, that is arrows elicited faster (left/right) button presses, whereas written words elicited faster vocal responses.

When these features co-occurred in the Stroop task, the interference arose when the S i corresponded to the fastest, most response-compatible dimension, consistent with both Response Speed and Translation accounts.

These findings were not consistent with the Reading Automaticity account, which predicts that word reading will dominate processing regardless of response modality and thus the strongest interference would occur when words are the S i .
Instead, we observed the opposite pattern: there was greater interference when the word was the target (S r ) and the arrow was the S i.

The results from the manual task diverge from the predictions of the DOM, which would instead predict that either response stimulus would elicit bidirectional interference compared to the asymmetry shown in the present study.

The DOM defines the manual arrowword Stroop task as having both S-S and S-R overlap, where the arrow does not share any greater spatial compatibility with the manual response than a written spatial word (Kornblum et al., 1990).
text.formatted: The DOM defines the manual arrowword Stroop task as having both S-S and S-R overlap, where the arrow does not share any greater spatial compatibility with the manual response than a written spatial word <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kornblum et al., 1990)</ref>.

text.text: Under this account, neither dimension should hold a compatibility advantage over the other in the manual task, and interference should therefore occur to a comparable degree regardless of which dimension is the S r .

Contrary to this prediction, we observed a clear asymmetry: interference and facilitation occurred only when the word was the S r and the arrow the S i , not the reverse, which is aligned with the findings of one other recent manual arrow-word Stroop study (Besner et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Contrary to this prediction, we observed a clear asymmetry: interference and facilitation occurred only when the word was the S r and the arrow the S i , not the reverse, which is aligned with the findings of one other recent manual arrow-word Stroop study <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Besner et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Although some manual arrow-word Stroop studies reported bidirectional interference (Baldo et al., 1998; Roelofs et al., 2006) the effect was not equivalent across dimensions as the DOM predicts, instead, interference found in the previous studies was consistently larger when the word was the S r .
text.formatted: Although some manual arrow-word Stroop studies reported bidirectional interference <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baldo et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Roelofs et al., 2006)</ref> the effect was not equivalent across dimensions as the DOM predicts, instead, interference found in the previous studies was consistently larger when the word was the S r .

text.text: Further, the observed asymmetry in the present task suggests that the spatial codes activated by arrows and words are not equivalent in strength for a manual response as the DOM would predict.

Instead, arrows appear to provide a highly compatible, automatic spatial cue that directly activates the manual response, whereas words activate spatial codes only indirectly, via semantic processing.

This additional translational step renders word responses vulnerable to the competing and automatic arrow-driven activation leading to interference, while arrow responses remain relatively insulated from competing word-driven activation when manually responding.

Although the present findings are consistent with the Translation Model, they may also be accommodated by accounts of graded compatibility between S-R dimensions (Braem et al., 2019; Lu & Proctor, 2001; Luo & Proctor, 2013).
text.formatted: Although the present findings are consistent with the Translation Model, they may also be accommodated by accounts of graded compatibility between S-R dimensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Braem et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lu & Proctor, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Luo & Proctor, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, interference reflects the relative strength of representational overlap and automatic cross-activation across domains, rather than a binary presence or absence of translation, as in the Translational Model.
For example, words indicating a direction may be compatible with a spatial manual response, however, this spatial compatibility may be less than that of the one between arrows and a manual response.

This account suggests that on the manual task, arrows possess maximal spatial compatibility with the response, generating strong, automatic activation that intrudes on responding to the word, whereas words activate spatial codes and generate comparatively weak competing activation failing to disrupt arrow responses (Luo & Proctor, 2013).
text.formatted: This account suggests that on the manual task, arrows possess maximal spatial compatibility with the response, generating strong, automatic activation that intrudes on responding to the word, whereas words activate spatial codes and generate comparatively weak competing activation failing to disrupt arrow responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Luo & Proctor, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In the vocal task, the reverse pattern occurs; coupling between words and speech, and weaker associations between arrows and linguistic responses, produces interference and facilitation only when responding to the arrow, not the word (Lu & Proctor, 2001; Braem et al., 2019; Luo & Proctor, 2013).
text.formatted: In the vocal task, the reverse pattern occurs; coupling between words and speech, and weaker associations between arrows and linguistic responses, produces interference and facilitation only when responding to the arrow, not the word <ref type="bibr">(Lu & Proctor, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Braem et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Luo & Proctor, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: This account could also be used to explain our asymmetrical interference effects observed in both tasks; whereby interference occurs when compatibility between the S r and the response is comparatively weaker than that of S i and the response.
Therefore, an S-R association account or the Translational model could both explain the pattern of interference and facilitation observed here in both the manual and vocal response tasks.

The findings highlight an important design principle for Stroop tasks: inhibitory demands are maximised when the most response-compatible stimulus is assigned as the S i , requiring participants to suppress the faster response in order to respond to the stimulus feature that requires cross-domain translation.

In the most commonly used manual Stroop task -the colour-word Stroop task -this criterion is not met as the ignored stimulus (word reading) does require translation across domains to a manual response, while responding to ink colour via an arbitrary button press is not necessarily slower.
This may explain the reduced magnitude of Stroop effects observed in manual versions of the colour-word Stroop task compared to the vocal iteration (Augustinova et al., 2019; Kinoshita et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This may explain the reduced magnitude of Stroop effects observed in manual versions of the colour-word Stroop task compared to the vocal iteration <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Augustinova et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Kinoshita et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, the manual arrow-word Stroop task studied here yielded robust interference effects when words were assigned as the S r and arrows as the S i.
Block structure also influenced performance.
Manual responses to words were faster when a congruent arrow was present in Pure blocks compared to the same congruent trials presented in Mixed blocks.
This aligns with previous research showing faster RTs to congruent stimuli in Pure blocks compared to those within Mixed blocks on Stroop tasks (Braem et al., 2019; Logan & Zbrodoff, 1979).
text.formatted: This aligns with previous research showing faster RTs to congruent stimuli in Pure blocks compared to those within Mixed blocks on Stroop tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Braem et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Logan & Zbrodoff, 1979)</ref>.

text.text: In Pure blocks of congruent trials, participants may adopt an alternative task-goal that either responding to the arrow or the word yields correct responses, leading to both components of the stimuli aiding in response selection.
Indeed, this may also explain why we observed faster RTs when words were presented with the congruent arrow in Pure blocks compared to the baseline word alone.
In contrast, in Mixed blocks, responses to words on congruent trials were not faster than the baseline word alone in the manual tasks.

This suggests that despite Mixed blocks containing a higher proportion of congruent trials relative to incongruent trials, the presence of a congruent arrow does not facilitate performance compared to the baseline word alone.

A similar pattern emerged in the vocal task, where responses to the arrow paired with a congruent word facilitated overall RT in Pure congruent blocks, but slowed overall RT in Mixed blocks, compared to the baseline arrow.
These findings indicate that the effect of block composition on goal-maintenance occur regardless of response modality.

In the manual task we observed that participants' responses to words in Mixed blocks with an incongruent arrow were significantly slower, and more erroneous, than their responses to the Pure-incongruent block.

One possibility is that in Mixed blocks the predominance of congruent trials strengthens reliance on the response-compatible dimension, increasing the need to maintain the task goal when an incongruent trial occurs.
This passive reinforcement of the unused response pathway may in turn weaken maintenance of the task goal (e.g., responding to the word).
This resulted in slowed responses to both congruent and incongruent trials, compared to when trials are completed in Pure blocks, as observed in both response modalities.

Inhibition is thought to not only require the ability to resolve interference at the trial level, but also to maintain task goals despite the presence of alternative goals (Bélanger et al., 2010; Cohen et al., 1992; Kane & Engle, 2003).
text.formatted: Inhibition is thought to not only require the ability to resolve interference at the trial level, but also to maintain task goals despite the presence of alternative goals <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bélanger et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cohen et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kane & Engle, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Given that participants were slower and made more errors on incongruent trials when responding manually to the word in Mixed conditions compared to Pure blocks, our findings support this view that inhibition reflects two concurrent mechanisms: resolving interference at the trial level and maintaining task goals across trials.
These findings support the use of the manual arrow-word Stroop task as a sensitive measure of inhibitory control in healthy adults.
This paradigm may be especially useful in evaluating inhibitory control in clinical groups, including those with, or at risk of, AD.
On the manual colour-word Stroop task, people with preclinical AD exhibited greater interference than age-matched healthy older adults (Hung et al., 2022).
text.formatted: On the manual colour-word Stroop task, people with preclinical AD exhibited greater interference than age-matched healthy older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hung et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, vocal responses to the colour-word Stroop task progressively impaired across healthy ageing, MCI, and AD groups (Bélanger et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Similarly, vocal responses to the colour-word Stroop task progressively impaired across healthy ageing, MCI, and AD groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bélanger et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the arrow-word Stroop task, which can be assessed online with manual keyboard responses may provide a practical and specific measure of inhibitory control.

It could be used in both healthy and clinical populations, without confounding speech-related factors such as articulation issues, vocal hesitations, difficulty with artificial intelligence (AI) transcription errors or age-related language change.
Our study had several limitations.
First, the manual and vocal tasks differed in their design, with manual task having trial-level data and the vocal task having block-level measures.
Thus, absolute response times were not compared directly across response modalities.

Instead, the analyses focused on within-task patterns of interference and facilitation relative to each task's own baseline conditions, as the primary objective was to determine whether the direction and magnitude of interference within each response modality were consistent with predictions from competing theoretical accounts.

Relatedly, because RT in the vocal task was recorded at the block level, the Mixed condition reflects an aggregate RT across congruent and incongruent trials within that block, precluding separate estimation of congruent-and incongruent-trial RT within Mixed blocks, unlike the trial-level manual data.

The vocal task required sequential responding across a visual array, whereas the manual task involved discrete trial-by-trial responses, and future work should determine whether presentation format contributes independently to interference patterns.
Secondly, using a written word as the response stimulus requires rapid word recognition, which may depend on a general reading or English-language fluency level.

Given that our participants were an educated, English-speaking, convenience sample, the impact of reading fluency was likely reflected in our relatively small proportion of errors and corrections observed in the vocal task.

Purely spatial Stroop tasks, such as the arrow-position Stroop (see Viviani et al., 2024 for review) which manipulates arrow direction and screen position (on the left or right side of the display; congruent or incongruent with arrow direction), may offer an alternative design that eliminates linguistic processing demands and isolates interference resolution within the spatial domain.
text.formatted: Purely spatial Stroop tasks, such as the arrow-position Stroop (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Viviani et al., 2024</ref> for review) which manipulates arrow direction and screen position (on the left or right side of the display; congruent or incongruent with arrow direction), may offer an alternative design that eliminates linguistic processing demands and isolates interference resolution within the spatial domain.

text.text: In summary, this study examined how stimulus-response mapping shapes interference and facilitation in the arrow-word Stroop task.
Across manual button-press and vocal paradigms, interference and facilitation were present when translation between stimulus and response domains was required.

This crossover pattern is consistent with the Translation and Response Speed accounts but challenges explanations based solely on word-reading automaticity and the bidirectional interference predicted by the DOM.
Further, Mixed-block designs may be better suited to assessing both interference resolution and maintaining tasklevel goal.

Together, these findings demonstrate that Stroop interference is determined not simply by the properties of the stimulus, but by the relationship between the relevant and irrelevant stimulus dimensions, the required response, and the broader task context.
